bug_description.original_source: ARVO-Meta report metadata plus staged sanitizer_trace.txt, patch.diff, and reproduction_report.json
bug_description.normalized: The staged witness `E8 03 FF` makes the fuzz harness compute `0xE8 % 33 == 1`, so it opens Capstone's X86 64-bit backend and passes the remaining two bytes `03 FF` into `cs_disasm()`. `cs_disasm()` allocates the returned `cs_insn` array with `malloc`, so each instruction's `id` field starts as uninitialized heap data. The X86 decoder accepts `03 FF` as one instruction and materializes an internal X86 opcode; the staged fix shows the matching missing public mapping is `X86_ADD32rr_REV -> X86_INS_ADD`. In the vulnerable revision, `X86_get_insn_id()` only assigns `insn->id` when `find_insn()` finds an entry in `insns[]`, but vulnerable `X86MappingInsn.inc` has `X86_ADD32rr` and not `X86_ADD32rr_REV`, so the write is skipped. `fill_insn()` does not repair the field because `OpcodePub` remains zero, and `cs_disasm()` then re-stores the still-uninitialized `id` at `insn_cache->id += mci.popcode_adjust`. The fuzzer later calls `cs_insn_name(handle, i->id)`, and `X86_insn_name()` first branches on and then indexes with that uninitialized scalar, producing the saved MemorySanitizer use-of-uninitialized-value at `arch/X86/X86Mapping.c:860`.

source.description: First non-harness project decode step that consumes the two attacker-controlled instruction bytes under the selected X86 64-bit backend and materializes the internal X86 opcode later looked up by `X86_get_insn_id()`.
source.value_from: `gt_results/arvo_13427/poc` is exactly three bytes: `E8 03 FF`. `0xE8 % 33 == 1` selects `platforms[1] = { CS_ARCH_X86, CS_MODE_64 }`, leaving `03 FF` as the instruction bytes that `decodeInstruction()` parses.

tainted_value_origin.description: The vulnerability-relevant value is the internal X86 opcode derived from witness bytes `03 FF` and stored into `mci.Opcode`. `cs_disasm()` later passes that opcode as `id` into `X86_get_insn_id()`.

root_cause.description: Root cause. `X86_get_insn_id()` writes the public instruction id only on a successful table lookup. For the exact witness path, the internal opcode exists in the X86 opcode enum but has no vulnerable `insns[]` entry, so `find_insn()` misses and this function leaves the heap `cs_insn.id` from `cs_disasm()` uninitialized.
root_cause.note: The vulnerable `arch/X86/X86MappingInsn.inc` lists `X86_ADD32rr, X86_INS_ADD, 0` but has no `X86_ADD32rr_REV` entry nearby; the staged fix inserts `X86_ADD32rr_REV, X86_INS_ADD, 0`. That added `_REV` mapping matches the witness bytes `03 FF` in X86 64-bit mode and explains why the vulnerable lookup skipped the `insn->id` assignment.

sink.description: MSan crash site. `X86_insn_name()` first compares the uninitialized instruction id against `X86_INS_ENDING` and then uses the same scalar as an index into `insn_name_maps`.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value` at `arch/X86/X86Mapping.c:860:6` in `X86_insn_name`, with callers `cs_insn_name` and `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` exactly matching this sink path.

parser_admitted.code: size_t count = cs_disasm(handle, Data+1, Size-1, address, 0, &all_insn);
parser_admitted.description: With `Size == 3` and `0xE8 % 33 == 1`, the harness opens the X86 64-bit backend and hands the exact bytes `03 FF` to `cs_disasm()`.

coarse_trace.summary: The harness uses selector byte `0xE8` to choose `platforms[1] = X86 64-bit` and passes the remaining bytes `03 FF` into `cs_disasm()`.
Capstone allocates a heap `cs_insn` buffer, decodes `03 FF` into an internal X86 opcode, and then tries to map that opcode to a public instruction id.
The vulnerable X86 mapping tables miss the witness opcode's public-id entry, so `X86_get_insn_id()` leaves `cs_insn.id` uninitialized and `fill_insn()` does not repair it.
The fuzzer later forwards the uninitialized `i->id` into `cs_insn_name()`, and `X86_insn_name()` consumes it as both a comparison operand and a name-table index, triggering the saved MSan report.

fine_trace.note: Harness step. The exact selector byte `0xE8` and `platforms_len == 33` make `i == 1`, so the harness selects `platforms[1] = { CS_ARCH_X86, CS_MODE_64 }` and sends the remaining bytes `03 FF` to `cs_disasm()`.

Allocation context. On this build `cs_mem_malloc` defaults to `malloc` (`cs.c:351`), so the returned `cs_insn` array is not zeroed. Before any later lookup writes to it, the first instruction object's `insn_cache->id` field is uninitialized heap data.

Source. Under the X86 64-bit backend, the exact bytes `03 FF` are accepted as one instruction and decoded into an internal X86 opcode. `translateInstruction()` immediately materializes that opcode into `mci.Opcode`, the value later passed to `X86_get_insn_id()`.

Root cause. `X86_get_insn_id()` only initializes `insn->id` on a table hit. For this witness, the vulnerable `insns[]` table has `X86_ADD32rr` but not the matching `_REV` entry added by the fix, so `find_insn()` misses and the heap `insn->id` from step 1 remains unwritten.

No fallback public id is supplied here. `MCInst_Init()` zeroed `OpcodePub` before decode, and this witness path never calls `MCInst_setOpcodePub()`, so the guard is false and `fill_insn()` leaves `insn->id` in the uninitialized state from steps 1 and 3.

Propagation to the returned instruction object. On this witness `mci.popcode_adjust` remains zero, so the `+=` still reads the uninitialized `insn_cache->id` and writes it back. The saved MSan trace identifies this line as the point where the uninitialized value was stored to memory.

Sink. The harness later forwards the returned `i->id` through `cs_insn_name()` into `X86_insn_name()`. This function first tests the uninitialized `id` against `X86_INS_ENDING` at line 860 and then uses the same scalar as an array index on line 863. The saved MSan trace reports the first use at line 860.

allocation_context.note: The saved MSan trace reports the uninitialized value as created by the heap allocation at this line; `cs_mem_malloc` is the default `malloc` on this build.

cross_validation.sink_matches_crash: Frame 0 of the saved MSan stack is `X86_insn_name` at `arch/X86/X86Mapping.c:860`, and its immediate callers `cs_insn_name` and `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` match the final sink path exactly.

cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The staged fix inserts the missing `_REV` X86 mapping entries, including `X86_ADD32rr_REV -> X86_INS_ADD`, so the witness opcode receives a public instruction id instead of flowing into `X86_insn_name()` as uninitialized heap data.

format.name: Capstone fuzz_disasmnext 3-byte X86 witness
format.contract: A 3-byte input whose first byte is exactly `0xE8`, so `Data[0] % 33 == 1` selects `platforms[1] = { CS_ARCH_X86, CS_MODE_64 }`, and whose remaining two bytes are exactly `03 FF`. Those two bytes must decode on the vulnerable X86 path that is missing the `_REV` add mapping entry, leaving `cs_insn.id` uninitialized before the harness calls `cs_insn_name(handle, i->id)`.
